newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW - HK firms in a whirl over listing abroad.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - HK firms in a whirl over listing abroad.

text.p: The prospect of snaring a higher price to earnings ratio (PER) in overseas markets has led to a wave of spinoffs by Hong Kong firms on overseas markets, where listing requirements also can be more lenient, analysts said.

"Strict restrictions here may encourage them to spinoff somewhere else," said Alex Tang, research director at Yamaichi International. "They can normally ask for a higher PER on an overseas exchange," he said.
Most recently Pacific Andes International Holdings Ltd spun off its frozen seafood trading business Pacific Andes (Holdings) Ltd, in Singapore. Trading in shares of the unit began on Friday.

Among planned spinoffs, IDT International Ltd said it planned to list its liquid crystal display products business in Singapore. Chung Hwa Development Holdings Ltd is planning to list its Leading Edge Packaging Inc unit in the United States and Regal Hotels International Holdings Ltd is considering a separate U.S. listing of its hotel operations.

"The companies (listing spinoffs abroad) are mainly industrial concerns, usually with very small market capitalisations," said Sunny Chan, senior research manager from Seapower Securities. "It is easier for them to meet overseas listing requirements than in Hong Kong."

The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong said in September it was mulling a tightening of its listing rules, preventing companies from spinning off their units during the first three years that they are listed in Hong Kong.
Analysts also said it was not easy for smaller companies to obtain sufficient bank credit in Hong Kong and seeking an overseas listing could provide easier access to funds.

"A higher PER means they can offer less shares but raise more capital. Seeking funding by overseas listings reduces their overall cost," said Michael Ng, senior analyst at ASG Investment Services. An overseas listing may also raise a firm's corporate profile, he added.

"Investors favour high-tech industrial stocks on overseas exchanges such as Singapore," added Stanley Ng, research manager at Mansion House. "They know how to evaluate the stocks and generally anticipate the industry's growth prospects better."
Ng said the Singapore government also encouraged the listing of high-tech industrial stocks and that helped companies obtain a higher PER.
"Hong Kong seems to favour services-oriented companies while Singapore favours high-tech firms," he said.

Analysts said the existence of various trading boards on some overseas exchanges to accommodate companies with different market capitalisations also meant that firms listing abroad could get a more favourable response from investors.

Herbert Hui, deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong exchange, has said he expects more Hong Kong companies to seek primary listings in Singapore ahead of the territory's mid-1997 handover to Chinese rule. He said this could enhance the international profile of Hong Kong companies.
Singapore is seen to be the most popular overseas exchange for a separate separate listing, followed by the United States.
Analysts said the move towards overseas listings seemed to have had very little impact on the initial public offering market in Hong Kong.
"There are still many new listings scheduled here," said Tang.
